sections.label: Content note
sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses the abuse of children in foster care, restraint, the drugging of children, and the deaths of children. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.heading: Not the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
Foster care is not part of the troubled teen industry, and Kids Over Profits does not track foster homes, foster care agencies or state child welfare systems. Children in foster care are in the custody of a state, county or tribal agency, placed there by a court. The agency, not a parent, decides where they live.

We made this page because the two systems share companies, buildings and children, and a history. State agencies send children in foster care to many of the same residential treatment centers that parents pay for, and some companies run both foster care programs and residential programs for teenagers. Orphanages, the orphan trains and the move to foster care are roots of both; that [history](#kop-ri-history) is told below.

We are not experts on foster care. The people who grew up in it, and the organizations listed below, are.

sections.label: What foster care is
sections.heading: What foster care is
sections.body:
On September 30, 2024, [328,947 children were in foster care](https://acf.gov/sites/default/files/documents/cb/2024-afcars-dashboard-printable.pdf) in the United States, and 505,682 spent some time in it during the 2024 federal fiscal year (preliminary federal AFCARS figures, published September 2025). On that day 39 percent lived with relatives or kin and 28 percent in non-relative foster homes. 28,365 children (9 percent) were in therapeutic foster homes. About 35,000 lived in group homes (13,234), institutions (7,555) or residential care (14,541). That number has fallen: residential facilities were the latest placement of [about 101,000 children in foster care (19 percent) in 2002 and about 34,000 (9 percent) in 2022](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-107625), according to the GAO ([our summary](/child-welfare/)).

Child welfare agencies spent [$34.3 billion in state fiscal year 2022](https://www.childtrends.org/publications/total-child-welfare-agency-spending-increased) from federal, state, local and other sources. [$9.5 billion of it](https://www.childtrends.org/publications/child-welfare-agencies-use-of-title-iv-e-funding-has-increased-since-2012) came from Title IV-E of the Social Security Act, the main federal foster care program. Treatment in residential facilities is also paid for by [Medicaid](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/rtf_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf), through per diem rates for each child.

### Private agencies

States hold custody but contract much of the work out. When the Senate Finance Committee surveyed the states in 2015, [31 of the 33 that answered](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CPRT-115SPRT26354/html/CPRT-115SPRT26354.htm) used private agencies to provide services to children in foster care, and 16 of them contracted with both for-profit and nonprofit providers. Private agencies recruit and supervise foster homes, run therapeutic foster care, and operate group homes, shelters and residential treatment programs.

### Group care after Family First

The Family First Prevention Services Act of 2018 [limits Title IV-E payments](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2024/many-states-lack-information-to-monitor-maltreatment-in-residential-facilities-for-children-in-foster-care/) for a child in a group setting to 14 days unless the setting meets certain requirements. One such setting is the Qualified Residential Treatment Program (QRTP). The Senate Finance Committee noted in 2024 that QRTPs [are not required to follow the same restraint and seclusion rules](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/rtf_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf) as psychiatric residential treatment facilities.

sections.label: History
sections.heading: Where foster care came from
sections.body:
Foster care grew out of centuries of taking poor children from their families and handing them to others to raise and to put to work. The same institutions, laws and ideas produced the orphanages, reform schools and residential programs the troubled teen industry came from.

### Children given away

The Roman father held [total legal power](/antiquity/) over his children, including the right to punish, sell or kill them. From the 6th century, parents gave children of 5 to 10, sometimes as young as 3, to monasteries as [oblates](/medieval-child-oblation-and-monastic-schools/), entered in charter books alongside gifts of land and livestock. The Rule of St. Benedict (529) obliged monasteries to provide for orphans; the Tenth Council of Toledo (656) forbade parents to take an oblate back.

### Put out to work

England's Vagabonds and Beggars Act of 1547 let authorities take begging children as young as seven off the streets, imprison or whip them, and place them in forced apprenticeships for up to ten years. The Poor Relief Act of 1572 and the Poor Law of 1601 let parish officials remove poor children from their parents and apprentice them. In 1627 English ships carried between 1,400 and 1,500 children to the American colonies as apprentice labor, an early case of "placing out" ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/)).

### Orphanages and houses of refuge

George Whitefield founded Bethesda Orphanage in 1740, the first in British America, citing the German Pietist August Hermann Francke, who believed a child's will must be broken to make the child obey. The Orphan Asylum Society of New York, founded in 1806 by philanthropists including Eliza Hamilton, gave children food, shelter and strict Protestant instruction while using their labor. Between 1800 and 1850 at least 62 private charities were created in the United States, most to place children in apprenticeships or indentured servitude ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/)).

The New York House of Refuge (1825) took children from "corrupting environments," especially immigrant neighborhoods, and held them for indeterminate terms of labor, corporal punishment and religious instruction, released when judged obedient. Boston and Philadelphia followed; Black children were excluded, segregated or sent to adult penitentiaries. The Philadelphia House of Refuge later became Glen Mills Schools, [closed in 2019](/juvenile-justice-timeline/) after widespread abuse allegations. In *Ex parte Crouse* (1838) the Pennsylvania Supreme Court upheld the state's right to institutionalize a child without due process for the child's "moral well-being," cementing the doctrine of *parens patriae*, the state as parent ([disability timeline](/idd-timeline/)). From 1841 Dorothea Dix documented children held with adults in almshouses, neglected and abused, and lobbied for separate institutions. New York's Children's Law of 1875 barred children aged 3 to 16 from county poorhouses and sent them to orphan asylums or to families approved by the State Board of Charities.

### The orphan trains

In 1854 Charles Loring Brace's Children's Aid Society of New York sent 46 children to Dowagiac, Michigan, the start of the orphan trains. An 1855 New York law let orphan asylums and children's homes "bind out" boys under 21 and girls under 18 with no limit on where. Many were not orphans: one charity's figures for 1857 to 1858 show that 65 percent of the children it placed had at least one living parent. In 1904 the New York Foundling Hospital sent 40 white children to Mexican Catholic families in the Arizona Territory; a white mob took the children, and the Arizona Supreme Court ruled in 1905 that their "best interests" required them to stay with Anglo families. In 1927, 12 states still allowed children from institutions and poor farms to be indentured. The last orphan train left New York for Sulphur Springs, Texas, on May 31, 1929 ([orphan care timeline](/orphanages/); [Trammell, *Orphan Train Myths and Legal Reality*](https://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/tma/vol5/iss2/3)).

### From orphanages to foster care and treatment

The 1909 White House Conference on Dependent Children declared care in a home preferable to an orphanage, and the shift toward foster care began. In 1917 Father Edward Flanagan opened a Catholic orphanage for boys in Nebraska that grew into Boys Town, a nonprofit running residential treatment and behavioral programs ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)). As orphanages emptied between the 1960s and 1980s, poor children moved into [psychiatric and behavioral facilities](/orphanages/). In July 1991 Straight in Boston, a branch of Straight, Inc., the Florida drug program founded in 1976, closed when Massachusetts pulled its foster care license.

Foster care also became an investment. Private equity firms bought The MENTOR Network in 2001; Vestar Capital Partners bought it in 2006 and took it public in 2014, and Centerbridge Partners and The Vistria Group took it private in 2019. It was renamed Sevita in 2021. Sequel Youth & Family Services, co-founded in 1999 by Jay Ripley, passed from one private equity owner to the next from 2010 ([corporatization timeline](/corporatization/)) and took in children from child welfare agencies across the country, as the next section describes.

sections.label: Where it meets the TTI
sections.heading: Where it meets the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
### The same facilities

Children reach residential treatment centers from parents, psychiatrists, schools, the juvenile justice system and [child welfare agencies](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/rtf_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf). The Senate Finance Committee's 2024 investigation of four large operators, Universal Health Services, Acadia Healthcare, Devereux Advanced Behavioral Health and Vivant Behavioral Healthcare, found that "a significant portion of foster children placed at RTFs have no demonstrated behavioral health needs." In 2013, it noted, 28.8 percent of children in congregate care had "No Clinical Indicators" ([our summary of the report](/warehouses-of-neglect/)).

All four are in our records: [Universal Health Services](/operator/universal-health-services/) with more than 70 programs, [Devereux](/operator/devereux-advanced-behavioral-health/) with 43, [Acadia Healthcare](/operator/acadia-healthcare/) with 13 and [Vivant Behavioral Health](/operator/vivant-behavioral-health/) with 5. So is [Sequel](/operator/sequel-tsi/), with 42 programs, most now closed. In 2020 APM Reports found that [more than 40 states and territories](https://www.apmreports.org/story/2020/09/28/for-profit-sequel-facilities-children-abused) had sent children to Sequel facilities in recent years.

### Companies that run both

- **Devereux** [recruits foster parents](https://www.devereux.org/site/PageServer?pagename=foster_care) and runs residential programs for children in several states.
- **KidsPeace** runs [foster care, residential campuses in Pennsylvania, Georgia and Maine, and a psychiatric hospital](https://www.kidspeace.org/services/) in Pennsylvania. Four of its programs are in our records.
- **Boys Town**, which began as a Catholic orphanage in Nebraska in 1917, runs [foster care](https://www.boystown.org/new-england/services/foster-care) and residential programs. Several of its programs are in our records.
- **Youth Villages** runs [foster care](https://youthvillages.org/services/foster-care/) and [five residential campuses](https://youthvillages.org/services/residential-services/) in Tennessee and Georgia, which are in our records.

### Sent out of state

In fiscal year 2021, [nearly 2,400 children](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2024/many-states-lack-information-to-monitor-maltreatment-in-residential-facilities-for-children-in-foster-care/) in foster care were placed in residential facilities in another state. The GAO recommended in 2022 that HHS help states share what works in preventing maltreatment in residential facilities. HHS agreed, but by June 2024 [had not acted](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-107625). The interstate compact that governs foster placements across state lines does not cover placements in residential treatment centers or group homes. ProPublica and the Chicago Tribune reported in 2020 that Illinois sent foster children to [Acadia-run facilities in Arkansas, Indiana and Michigan](https://www.propublica.org/article/illinois-dcfs-children-out-of-state-placements) where police logs recorded assaults and sexual abuse reports. Oregon [brought all its out-of-state foster children home](https://www.opb.org/news/article/oregon-brings-back-all-foster-children-placed-out-of-state/) in June 2020 and ended its contract with Sequel, which held most of them.

### The same practices

In 2020 a 16-year-old in foster care died after staff at Lakeside Academy, a Sequel facility in Michigan, [restrained him on the floor for about 12 minutes](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/video-shows-fatal-restraint-cornelius-fredericks-16-michigan-foster-facility-n1233122). The medical examiner ruled his death a homicide. The Senate Finance Committee described a 14-year-old Oregon foster child with an intellectual disability who was [physically restrained and chemically sedated more than 30 times in four months](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/rtf_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf) at UHS's Provo Canyon School in Utah.

### The same people

Vivant was founded in 2021 by Jay Ripley, who had co-founded Sequel in 1999 and, before that, the juvenile justice contractor Youth Services International, later owned and run by James F. Slattery ([juvenile justice timeline](/juvenile-justice-timeline/)). In 2021 Sequel sold 13 facilities to Vivant. The same committee found that three senior leaders of Vivant had come from Sequel, including its former vice president of operations, who joined Vivant in 2021, a month after leaving Sequel. Ripley told an interviewer in 2015 that Sequel sought children whose placements the government pays for, and that "you can make money in this business if you control staffing" ([Senate Finance Committee, 2024](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/rtf_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf); [our summary](/warehouses-of-neglect/)).

### Nowhere to go

When no placement is found, children wait. Kentucky's ombudsman reviewed 49 children who [slept in state office buildings](https://auditor.ky.gov/PressRoom/Pages/Auditor-Ball-Receives-Alarming-Report-on-Foster-Children-Housed-in-Office-Buildings-Across-Commonwealth.aspx) between June and October 2024. The longest stay was 35 days and the youngest child was one year old. A shortage of placements is also the reason states give for sending children to facilities in other states.

sections.label: What investigations have found
sections.heading: What investigations have found
sections.body:
- **States cannot see patterns of abuse (HHS Office of Inspector General, 2024).** [16 states](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2024/many-states-lack-information-to-monitor-maltreatment-in-residential-facilities-for-children-in-foster-care/) lacked the information to identify patterns of maltreatment in residential facilities. 32 did not formally track whether a facility's owner ran facilities in other states. 13 states did not consistently report whether a maltreated child lived in a residential facility, so the Inspector General could not count abuse in these facilities nationwide.
- **Harm built into the business (Senate Finance Committee, 2024).** The committee's report, [*Warehouses of Neglect*](https://www.finance.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/rtf_report_warehouses_of_neglect.pdf), ([our summary](/warehouses-of-neglect/)), found that providers fill facilities to capacity while cutting staff to maximize per diem margins, and that the resulting harms, including abuse by staff and overused restraint and seclusion, are "endemic to the RTF operating model."
- **A for-profit foster care company (Senate Finance Committee, 2017).** The committee studied [The MENTOR Network](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CPRT-115SPRT26354/html/CPRT-115SPRT26354.htm), then majority owned by the private equity firm Vestar Capital Partners and serving 10,300 foster children in 18 states. Maryland found violations in 20 of 22 quarterly reviews and MENTOR kept operating there. Most children who died in its care were never the subject of an internal investigation. Its foster care now operates under the name [Sevita](https://sevitahealth.com/our-services/families/foster-care/) ([its owners since 2001](#kop-ri-history)).
- **Sequel (APM Reports, 2020).** Reporters compiled [more than 8,600 emergency calls](https://www.apmreports.org/story/2020/09/28/for-profit-sequel-facilities-children-abused) from Sequel facilities in 18 states and found 20 cases since 2010 in which government investigators found staff in sexual or romantic relationships with residents.
- **Devereux (2020).** After a Philadelphia Inquirer investigation reported a 25-year pattern of sexual abuse by staff, Philadelphia's child welfare and behavioral health agencies [moved to remove 53 children](https://whyy.org/articles/philly-removes-children-from-devereux-facilities-after-sex-abuse-revelations/) from Devereux facilities.
- **Psychotropic drugs.** The GAO found in 2011 that foster children in five states were [prescribed psychotropic drugs at higher rates](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-12-201) than other children on Medicaid, that hundreds took five or more at once, and that some infants were prescribed them. In 2018 the Inspector General found that [one in three foster children](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2018/treatment-planning-and-medication-monitoring-were-lacking-for-children-in-foster-care-receiving-psychotropic-medication/) on these drugs in five states did not get the treatment planning or monitoring their states required.
- **What young people say (Think of Us, 2021).** In [*Away From Home*](https://www.thinkofus.org/case-studies/away-from-home), 78 young people who had lived in group homes, shelters and residential treatment while in foster care described their placements. The authors concluded that most "found little to no long term value from them."

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If a child is in danger right now**, call [911](tel:911).
- **State child protective services (CPS):** every state has a line for reports of child abuse and neglect, including abuse in foster homes, group homes and residential facilities. Find yours in the federal [list of state reporting numbers](https://www.childwelfare.gov/state-child-abuse-and-neglect-reporting-numbers/). Abuse in a facility is investigated by the state where the facility is, so a child placed out of state is reported there. Tell the child's caseworker and the agency that placed the child as well.
- **Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline**, call or text, 24 hours, in more than 170 languages: 1-800-422-4453. Childhelp counselors are not a reporting line themselves; they can help you work out what to do and reach the right agency.
- **Protection and Advocacy agencies:** every state has a federally mandated legal advocacy agency for people with disabilities, including children harmed in residential treatment centers and hospitals. [Find your state's agency](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline**, 24 hours: call or text [988](tel:988).

Our [reporting directory](/report-abuse/) lists each state's agencies, hotlines and licensing offices.

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [FosterClub](https://www.fosterclub.com/): A national network for young people in and from foster care, "built for youth, powered by youth," whose Lived Experience Leaders speak to lawmakers and agencies.
- [Foster Youth in Action](https://www.fosteryouthaction.org/): Founded in 2008 by foster youth organizers. A national network of youth-led groups working to change the foster care system.
- [Think of Us](https://www.thinkofus.org/): A foster care research and policy organization led and guided by people with lived experience. Publisher of *Away From Home*, on institutional placements.
- [Children's Rights](https://www.childrensrights.org/): Brings legal action against state systems, including to stop the unnecessary institutionalization of children.
- [National Center for Youth Law](https://youthlaw.org/): Impact litigation and policy work on foster care, youth justice, health and education.
- [Juvenile Law Center](https://jlc.org/): Advocates for the rights of young people in the child welfare and justice systems.
- [The Imprint](https://imprintnews.org/): An independent nonprofit daily newsroom covering child welfare and youth justice, including its "Medicated in Foster Care" series.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you grew up in foster care, work in it, or know something on this page is wrong or out of date, please [tell us](/contact/). We will correct it.
